notes.meaning: Josiah became king when he was only eight years old, following the assassination of his father. He ruled Judah from Jerusalem for thirty-one years. His mother Jedidah likely helped guide him toward godliness during his childhood.
Josiah lived faithfully before the Lord throughout his reign. He followed the godly example of his ancestor King David, obeying God's laws without straying into idolatry or sin.
When Josiah had reigned for eighteen years, he took action to restore the temple. He sent Shaphan, the royal court secretary, to lead this project at the house of the Lord.

Josiah directed Shaphan to tell Hilkiah the high priest to count the silver that the people had given at the temple gates. This money had been gathered by the priests at the entrance over many years to fund repairs.
The gathered money was to be placed into the hands of the project overseers. These supervisors would then pay the laborers who were repairing the broken and neglected parts of the temple.
The funds paid the wages of carpenters, builders, and masons. The money also bought the timber and cut stone required to rebuild the damaged structure.
The king did not require an audit or financial report from the supervisors. They were trusted completely because they carried out their work with honesty and integrity.

While the temple was being cleaned and repaired, Hilkiah found the Book of the Law and gave it to Shaphan. This scroll contained the sacred laws of Moses that had been neglected during years of idolatry.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Many historical critics argue that this scroll was not an ancient Mosaic text, but an early edition of Deuteronomy composed around this time to promote centralized worship in Jerusalem.

notes.meaning: Shaphan returned to the king and reported on his original task. He told Josiah that the temple funds had been counted and handed over to the supervisors and workmen.
Shaphan then presented the newly found scroll to Josiah. He read portions of the book aloud in the king's presence, including the warnings of judgment for breaking God's covenant.
As Josiah heard the warnings written in the law, he tore his clothes. Tearing one's clothing was an ancient expression of deep grief, terror, and sorrow over sin.
Josiah immediately sent a delegation of trusted royal officials, including Hilkiah the high priest and Shaphan the scribe, on an urgent mission.

The king commanded his officials to seek the Lord's will for himself and the nation. He recognized that Judah stood under God's severe wrath because their ancestors had disobeyed the commands written in the scroll.

The officials consulted Huldah the prophetess, who lived in the Second District of Jerusalem. She was recognized as a faithful spokesperson for the Lord and was close at hand while other prophets were elsewhere.

differ.view: Women may hold any teaching or governing office in the church, as shown by God appointing women like Huldah to speak His authoritative word to high leaders.
Pastoral governing and teaching offices in the church remain reserved for men, because Old Testament prophetic messages delivered by women were occasional and distinct from congregational eldership.

notes.meaning: Huldah spoke with direct divine authority, delivering God's words without flattering the royal court. She referred to Josiah simply as the man who sent the messengers, showing that even kings answer to the Lord.
The Lord confirmed that severe judgment was coming upon Jerusalem and its inhabitants. The curses and disasters written in the Book of the Law would certainly come to pass.

God explained why this judgment was final: the people had abandoned Him to burn incense to false gods. By bowing to idols made by their own hands, they provoked God's wrath, which could no longer be quenched.
Huldah then delivered a separate, gracious word intended specifically for King Josiah. The Lord had taken note of the king's sincere reaction to the reading of the law.
God noted that Josiah's heart was soft and responsive, not hardened in pride. Because the king wept, tore his clothes, and humbled himself upon hearing the warnings, the Lord heard his prayer.

The Lord promised that Josiah would be gathered to his grave in peace before the destruction came. Although Josiah later fell in battle, he died in peace with God and was spared the anguish of seeing Jerusalem destroyed and taken into exile.
